problems.title: Seed Bank Tally
problems.story: A seed bank takes in packets all season, each stamped with a variety code. The curator wants to know how many packets the commonest variety accounted for — not which variety it was, just how many packets carried it.
problems.statement:
You are given the code stamped on each packet, in the order the packets arrived.

Return the number of packets carrying the commonest code. If two codes tie, both counts are equal, so return that count.

A season with no packets returns 0.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one packet’s variety code, in the order the packets arrived. The season may have brought no packets at all.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of packets carrying the commonest code; return 0 when no packets arrived.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: Equal values represent the same observation.

examples.explanation: Code 11 is stamped on three packets, code 4 on two and code 7 on one. The commonest is 11, so the answer is three.
No packets arrived all season, so no code has a count at all and the answer is zero.

testCases.explanation: Applying the maximum frequency rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the maximum frequency rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Record how often each distinct value has appeared.
The answer changes only when one stored count exceeds the current maximum.

editorial.overview: Maintain a frequency table while scanning the observations once, and retain the largest count reached.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For every position, scan the full array and count equal values, then take the largest count.
editorial.optimalApproach: Use a hash table from value to count. Increment one entry for each observation and update a running maximum.
editorial.correctnessProof: After processing any prefix, the table stores the exact count of every value in that prefix. The running maximum is therefore the greatest prefix count. After the full array it is exactly the requested maximum frequency.

c11.referenceSolution:
int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(!n)return 0;long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*n);memcpy(a,v,sizeof(long long)*n);qsort(a,n,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);long long best=1,run=1;for(int i=1;i<n;i++){run=a[i]==a[i-1]?run+1:1;if(run>best)best=run;}free(a);return best;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){unordered_map<long long,long long>f;long long best=0;for(auto x:v)best=max(best,++f[x]);return best;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){Map<Long,Long>f=new HashMap<>();long best=0;for(long x:v){long n=f.getOrDefault(x,0L)+1;f.put(x,n);best=Math.max(best,n);}return best;}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){const f=new Map();let b=0;for(const x of v){const n=(f.get(x)||0)+1;f.set(x,n);b=Math.max(b,n);}return b;}

problems.title: Cold Store Aisle Sweep
problems.story: A cold store numbers its aisles outward from the central corridor. The corridor itself is aisle 0, aisles on one side run negative, aisles on the other run positive. During a stock-take a worker logs each aisle as they finish it, in whatever order the aisles happened to be walked. An aisle can be logged more than once if two people covered it, and plenty are never reached at all. What the manager needs before signing off is not how many aisles were done, but the largest stretch that can be certified as a whole.
problems.statement:
You are given the aisle numbers from the log.

An unbroken block is a set of consecutively numbered aisles where every aisle in the set appears in the log at least once. A block with a hole anywhere in it is not unbroken. A single logged aisle is an unbroken block of one.

Return the number of aisles in the largest unbroken block.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one aisle that was logged. They appear in the order the aisles were walked, which carries no meaning here. The same aisle may appear any number of times, and the log may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of aisles in the largest unbroken block of consecutively numbered aisles that were all logged. Return 0 for an empty log.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Every aisle number recorded in the stock-take log, in the order it was walked.

constraints: The same aisle number may appear any number of times
The log may be empty, in which case the answer is 0

examples.explanation: The log covers aisles 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 9. Aisles 1 through 4 form an unbroken block of four. Aisle 7 and aisle 9 each stand alone, because 5, 6 and 8 were never logged.
One aisle walked four times is still one aisle. The largest unbroken block has a single member, so the answer is one rather than four.
Aisles -2, -1, 0 and 1 run consecutively across the corridor, which is a block of four. Aisle 3 is cut off because aisle 2 was never logged.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: aisles 1 through 4 are the largest unbroken block.
A block that runs across the corridor from negative aisles into positive ones.
An empty log. Catches a solution that assumes at least one aisle, or that starts its best-so-far at one.
The smallest non-empty log, holding the most negative aisle allowed.
Both constraint extremes present. The two largest aisle numbers are consecutive; the most negative one is isolated.
Seven entries covering four aisles. A solution that measures the run by counting log entries rather than distinct aisles reports 7.
Every entry is the same aisle, so the largest block holds one aisle.
Two blocks interleaved in the log, three aisles and four. Order of logging must not decide the answer.

hints: The order the aisles were walked carries no meaning, so any solution that depends on it is solving a different problem.
Membership is the only question you ever ask of the log: is this aisle number in it or not. A structure that answers that in constant time is the whole tool.
Walking upward from every logged aisle re-walks the same block once per member. Ask which single aisle in a block is worth starting from.
An aisle whose immediate lower neighbour was also logged can never be the bottom of a block, so it is never worth starting a count there.

editorial.overview: The log is a bag of aisle numbers whose order and repetitions carry no information, so the first move is to reduce it to the set of aisles that appear at all. The question then becomes a question about that set: how long is its longest run of consecutive integers.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Put every aisle in a set, then from each aisle walk upward while the next number is present, and keep the longest walk. Without a guard this re-walks a block of length k once from every one of its k members, which is quadratic on a single long block and times out at two hundred thousand aisles.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep the same set, but only start counting at an aisle whose immediate lower neighbour is absent. Such an aisle is the bottom of its block, every block has exactly one bottom, and so every block is walked exactly once. The total work across all walks is therefore the size of the set rather than its square, giving O(n) expected time with a hash set. Sorting the distinct aisles and scanning for consecutive steps is a correct alternative at O(n log n), which also fits comfortably inside the limit.
editorial.correctnessProof: Consider any unbroken block in the set and let b be its smallest member. Then b - 1 is absent, so b is a starting aisle and the walk from b counts the whole block. Conversely a walk started at any aisle a stops as soon as it meets a gap, so it never counts an aisle outside the block containing a, and it never overcounts. Every block therefore contributes its exact length exactly once, and taking the maximum over starting aisles gives the largest block. Duplicates cannot affect the result because the set holds each aisle once, which is why reducing the log to a set is a step of the argument and not an optimisation.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected, where n is the number of logged entries. Each distinct aisle is visited at most twice: once as a candidate start, once inside a single walk.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the set of distinct aisles.

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Second hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. problems.title: Kiln Soak Window
problems.story: A studio kiln carries a probe that records the chamber temperature once a minute, from the first flame to the last. Some glazes need a soak: a stretch of the firing where the heat is held as steady as the kiln can manage. What matters to the glaze is not how hot the soak runs. It is how little the temperature moves while the soak lasts.
problems.statement:
You are given a soak length in minutes, followed by the temperature log in the order the probe recorded it.

For any stretch of consecutive readings exactly as long as the soak, call its spread the highest reading in that stretch minus the lowest. A perfectly steady stretch has a spread of zero.

Return the smallest spread of any stretch in the log whose length is exactly the soak length.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the soak length in minutes. Every number after it is one temperature reading, in the order the probe recorded them. The log always holds at least as many readings as the soak is long.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest spread found among all stretches of readings exactly as long as the soak.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The soak length in minutes, followed by the temperature log in recording order.

constraints: The log holds n = values.length - 1 readings, and 1 <= soak length <= n
The answer can exceed the range of a 32-bit signed integer: a log holding both extremes has a spread of 2000000000

examples.explanation: The five stretches of three readings have spreads 3, 14, 14, 4 and 2. The steadiest is the last one, 1052 1051 1053, which moves by two degrees.
A one-minute soak is a single reading, and a single reading cannot move. Every stretch has a spread of zero, so the smallest is zero.
The soak is as long as the whole log, so there is exactly one stretch to consider. Its hottest reading is 1205 and its coolest is 1180, a spread of twenty-five degrees.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: the last three readings move by two degrees.
Soak length equals the log length, so one stretch is the whole log.
The smallest legal input: one reading and a one-minute soak. Catches an implementation that assumes at least two readings.
Both constraint extremes in one stretch. The answer exceeds a 32-bit signed integer.

Every early stretch spans two billion while the answer is two. A solution holding the spread in a 32-bit int overflows on the early stretches and reports a negative value smaller than the true answer.
Every reading is identical, so every stretch is perfectly steady. Catches a deque that mishandles ties when popping.
The steadiest pair is the repeated 6, in the middle rather than at either end.

hints: Every stretch you consider has exactly the same length, so as you step forward one reading joins the stretch and one leaves it.
You never need the whole stretch, only its hottest and coolest reading. Ask what it costs to keep just those two up to date.
A reading that is cooler than one arriving after it can never be the hottest reading of any later stretch. That observation lets you discard it permanently.
Keep two queues of positions, one whose readings decrease and one whose readings increase, and drop the front of each when it falls out of the stretch.

editorial.overview: The stretches all have the same length and move one reading at a time, which is the shape of a sliding window. The work is keeping the hottest and coolest reading of the current window available in constant time, because recomputing them from scratch is what makes the naive solution too slow.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Take every starting position, scan its whole stretch, and track the largest and smallest reading you see. That is O(n * w) time and O(1) extra space. It is correct and it is fine for a short log, but with two hundred thousand readings and a soak half that long it performs roughly ten billion comparisons.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep two double-ended queues of positions rather than values. The first holds positions whose readings strictly decrease from front to back, so its front is always the hottest reading of the current window. The second holds positions whose readings increase, so its front is the coolest. When a reading arrives, pop from the back of each queue while the arriving reading beats what is there, then push its position. Afterwards drop the front of either queue if it has fallen out of the window. Once the first full window is complete, its spread is the difference of the two fronts, and the answer is the smallest such difference. Each position is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is O(n) time and O(n) space.
editorial.correctnessProof: Take the maximum queue. If position i is in the window and some later position j in the window holds a reading at least as hot, then i can never be the answer for this window or any later one, because every later window containing i also contains j. Popping i is therefore safe. What remains is exactly the set of positions not dominated by any later position in the window, and the front of that set is the earliest, which is the current maximum. The minimum queue is the same argument with the comparison reversed. Since the fronts are the true maximum and minimum of each window, the spread computed for each window is exact, and taking the smallest over all windows gives the answer.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the number of readings. Each position enters and leaves each queue at most once.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the two queues of positions, which together hold at most n entries.

problems.title: Museum Ticket Pair Count
problems.story: Museum Ticket Pair Count is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise distinct target pairs result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Museum Ticket Pair Count. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the distinct target pairs, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is the target. The remaining elements form the collection to pair.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of distinct unordered value pairs whose sum equals the target.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: A pair uses two different positions; equal-value pairs need two copies.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 3.
Example 2 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.

testCases.explanation: Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Sort the collection and place one pointer at each end.
Move both pointers after a match and skip repeated values so a value pair is counted once.

editorial.overview: Sort the payload values, then converge two pointers according to whether their sum is below, above, or equal to the target.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every pair of positions and store matching value pairs in a set to remove duplicates.
editorial.optimalApproach: A sorted two-pointer scan counts each distinct complement pair once while skipping equal neighbors.
editorial.correctnessProof: At each step, a sum below target cannot be repaired by decreasing the right value, so advancing left loses no solution; the symmetric argument holds above target. A match is counted once and duplicate values are skipped, so every distinct pair appears exactly once.

c11.referenceSolution:
int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(n<3)return 0;long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*(n-1));memcpy(a,v+1,sizeof(long long)*(n-1));qsort(a,n-1,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);int l=0,r=n-2;long long c=0;while(l<r){long long s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;long long x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}free(a);return c;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){if(v.empty())return 0;auto a=vector<long long>(v.begin()+1,v.end());sort(a.begin(),a.end());int l=0,r=(int)a.size()-1;long long c=0;while(l<r){auto s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;auto x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}return c;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){if(v.length==0)return 0;long[]a=Arrays.copyOfRange(v,1,v.length);Arrays.sort(a);int l=0,r=a.length-1;long c=0;while(l<r){long s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;long x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}return c;}

python3.referenceSolution:
def solve(v: list[int]) -> int:
    if not v: return 0
    t,a=v[0],sorted(v[1:]);l,r,c=0,len(a)-1,0
    while l<r:
        s=a[l]+a[r]
        if s==t:
            c+=1;x,y=a[l],a[r]
            while l<r and a[l]==x:l+=1
            while l<r and a[r]==y:r-=1
        elif s<t:l+=1
        else:r-=1
    return c

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;const t=v[0],a=v.slice(1).sort((x,y)=>x-y);let l=0,r=a.length-1,c=0;while(l<r){const s=a[l]+a[r];if(s===t){c++;const x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]===x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]===y)r--;}else if(s<t)l++;else r--;}return c;}

problems.title: Sorted Dock Insertion
problems.story: Sorted Dock Insertion is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise first valid sorted position result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Sorted Dock Insertion. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the first valid sorted position, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is the query target. values[1..] is a nondecreasing sorted sequence.
problems.outputFormat: Return the zero-based position inside the sorted sequence where target first could appear.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: values[1..] is sorted in nondecreasing order
The answer may equal the sequence length.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated first valid sorted position process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.
Example 2 follows the stated first valid sorted position process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.

testCases.explanation: Applying the first valid sorted position rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the first valid sorted position rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Maintain a half-open search interval [low, high).
When the middle value is at least the target, keep the middle position in the candidate interval.

editorial.overview: Binary search for the first element that is not smaller than the target, using the sequence after the first input cell.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Scan from the beginning until an element is at least the target.
editorial.optimalApproach: Repeatedly halve a half-open interval. Move high to mid when the middle is large enough; otherwise move low past mid.
editorial.correctnessProof: All indices below low are known smaller than target and every valid answer remains below high. Each update preserves these invariants and shrinks the interval. At low = high, that index is the first possible insertion position.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(!n)return 0;int l=1,r=n;while(l<r){int m=l+(r-l)/2;if(v[m]>=v[0])r=m;else l=m+1;}return l-1;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){if(v.length==0)return 0;int l=1,r=v.length;while(l<r){int m=(l+r)>>>1;if(v[m]>=v[0])r=m;else l=m+1;}return l-1;}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;let l=1,r=v.length;while(l<r){const m=(l+r)>>1;if(v[m]>=v[0])r=m;else l=m+1;}return l-1;}

problems.title: Ferry Weight Rating
problems.story: A vehicle ferry runs a fixed number of crossings a day. Vehicles wait on the slipway in a single queue and board strictly in that order, because the queue is the fairness rule and nobody is waved past anyone else. Each crossing takes as many vehicles from the front as will fit, then sails. The operator is buying a replacement ferry and has to state a weight rating: too small and the queue will not clear by nightfall, too large and they are paying for a boat they do not need.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of crossings available and the weight of each vehicle in queue order.

Every vehicle must cross today. Vehicles board in queue order, so each crossing carries a run of vehicles taken from the front of what remains. A crossing may carry any number of vehicles as long as their combined weight does not exceed the ferry rating.

Return the smallest weight rating that gets every vehicle across within the available crossings.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many crossings the ferry can make today. Every number after it is the weight of one vehicle in kilograms, in the order the vehicles stand in the queue.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest weight rating that clears the whole queue within the available crossings.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The number of crossings available, followed by the weight of each vehicle in queue order.

constraints: The queue holds n = values.length - 1 vehicles, and 1 <= crossings <= n
The answer can exceed the range of a 32-bit signed integer: one crossing carrying a full queue may total 200000000000000

examples.explanation: With a rating of 70 the crossings carry 40 and 30, then 50 and 20, then 60 and 10, which is three crossings exactly. A rating of 69 forces the first crossing to take only the 40, and the queue no longer clears in three.
Six crossings for six vehicles means each can sail alone, so the rating only has to carry the heaviest single vehicle. No rating below 60 works at all, because that vehicle could never board.
One crossing must carry the entire queue, so the rating is the total weight of every vehicle waiting.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: three crossings of 70 kilograms each.
A single crossing, so the rating is the whole queue at once.
The smallest legal input: one crossing and one vehicle. Catches a search whose bounds collapse wrongly when they start equal.
One crossing carrying three vehicles at the maximum weight. The answer exceeds a 32-bit signed integer, and so does the upper bound of the search.
One crossing per vehicle, so the answer is the heaviest single vehicle.
Six identical vehicles over three crossings, two per crossing. Catches an off-by-one that returns 13 and leaves a vehicle behind.

The lower-bound trap. Total weight is 104 over five crossings, so a search starting from the average of 21 returns a rating that the 100 kilogram vehicle could never board on. The search must start at the heaviest single vehicle.
Five vehicles over two crossings splits three and two, so the rating is 15 rather than the 13 an even division of the total would suggest.

hints: A bigger ferry never makes the queue harder to clear. Convince yourself of that first, because everything else depends on it.
For a rating you have already picked, counting the crossings it needs is easy: fill each one from the front until the next vehicle will not fit, then sail.
That counting test answers yes for every rating above some threshold and no for every rating below it. The answer is exactly that threshold.
The candidate ratings are not in the input. They run from some lowest sensible rating up to the total weight of the queue, and you are searching that range rather than the array.
The lowest sensible rating is not the average load per crossing. A vehicle heavier than the rating can never board at all, so the range starts at the heaviest single vehicle.

editorial.overview: The queue order is fixed and every crossing takes a run from the front, so a rating determines the whole schedule: fill each crossing until the next vehicle will not fit. That makes the number of crossings a function of the rating alone, and the question becomes finding the smallest rating whose crossing count fits the budget.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every candidate rating from the heaviest vehicle upward and stop at the first that clears the queue in time. Each trial costs one sweep of the queue. It is correct and hopeless: the range of candidates reaches two hundred billion thousand, so even at one sweep per candidate this never finishes.
editorial.optimalApproach: Binary search the rating. The search space is not the input array but the interval from the heaviest single vehicle up to the total weight of the queue, because no smaller rating can carry the heaviest vehicle and no larger rating is ever needed. For a candidate rating, sweep the queue once with a running load, starting a new crossing whenever the next vehicle would overflow, and compare the crossings used against the budget. If it fits, the answer is at most this rating, so move the upper bound down to it; otherwise move the lower bound above it. The loop ends with the bounds equal on the smallest rating that fits. One sweep per step gives O(n log S) time, where S is the total weight, and O(1) extra space.
editorial.correctnessProof: The greedy sweep is optimal for a fixed rating. Suppose some schedule uses fewer crossings than the sweep. Compare them from the front: the sweep puts at least as many vehicles on the first crossing as any valid schedule can, because it only stops when the next vehicle would overflow, so after the first crossing the sweep has cleared a prefix at least as long. Repeating the argument, the sweep is never behind after any crossing, so it cannot finish later. Therefore the crossings it counts is the true minimum for that rating. Monotonicity follows: raising the rating never causes the sweep to start a crossing earlier, so the crossing count never increases. The predicate is therefore false below a threshold and true at and above it, which is exactly what binary search needs, and the bounds are valid because the heaviest vehicle must fit on some crossing and the total weight always fits in one.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log S), where n is the number of vehicles and S the total weight. One sweep of the queue per binary-search step.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the input, since the sweep only carries a running load and a count.

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Fourth hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. Binary searching over an answer space with a greedy feasibility predicate is a standard technique and is named openly in the editorial; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Labelled hard rather than medium because the existing binary-search group searches inside the given array, while this one requires constructing a search space that appears nowhere in the input and proving the predicate monotone. The counter-argument, that binary search is the topic’s own tool and so should not count as a step up, is recorded here because the call is close.

problems.title: Silo Row Banner
problems.story: A co-operative wants to paint one rectangular advert across the front of its grain silos. The silos stand in a row, each one unit wide but built to different heights. The advert has to be a single rectangle spanning whole neighbouring silos, and it cannot rise above the shortest silo it covers.
problems.statement:
You are given the height of each silo, left to right.

Pick any run of neighbouring silos. The biggest rectangle that run allows is as wide as the run and as tall as its shortest silo.

Return the largest area any run allows. No silos means no advert, so 0.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one silo’s height, in the order the silos stand. Every silo is one unit wide, and the row may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return the largest rectangular area that can be painted across a run of neighbouring silos.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: The result fits in a signed 64-bit integer.

examples.explanation: The last three silos are all 7 tall, so that run is three wide and 7 high, giving 21. The two 4s give only 8, and spanning all six silos caps the height at 2 for 12.
The 6-tall silo on its own gives 6. Spanning both silos would cap the height at 2, for an area of only 4.

testCases.explanation: Applying the largest contiguous rectangle rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the largest contiguous rectangle rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: A bar can extend until the first smaller bar on each side.
Use a monotonic increasing stack and finalize taller bars when a shorter bar arrives.

editorial.overview: Use a monotonic stack of starting positions and heights. Each pop finalizes the widest rectangle for that height.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Choose every left boundary, extend right, maintain the minimum height, and evaluate each rectangle.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep increasing heights with their earliest valid starts. A lower height closes all taller rectangles; a zero sentinel closes the rest.
editorial.correctnessProof: A popped height cannot extend through the current lower bar, and its stored start is the earliest position it can reach. Thus the computed width is maximal for that height. Every height is eventually popped, so the best rectangle is considered.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){long long best=0,*h=malloc(sizeof(long long)*(n+1));int*s=malloc(sizeof(int)*(n+1)),top=0;for(int i=0;i<=n;i++){long long x=i<n?v[i]:0;int start=i;while(top&&h[top-1]>x){top--;if(h[top]*(i-s[top])>best)best=h[top]*(i-s[top]);start=s[top];}if(!top||h[top-1]<x){h[top]=x;s[top++]=start;}}free(h);free(s);return best;}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){const st=[];let b=0;for(let i=0;i<=v.length;i++){const h=i<v.length?v[i]:0;let s=i;while(st.length&&st[st.length - 1][1]>h){const p=st.pop();b=Math.max(b,p[1]*(i-p[0]));s=p[0];}if(!st.length||st[st.length - 1][1]<h)st.push([s,h]);}return b;}

problems.title: Strait Ice Floes
problems.story: A narrow strait carries floating ice. Opposing currents run along it, so each floe is driven either east or west, and every floe drifts at the same speed. When two floes closing on each other meet, the heavier one carries on as if nothing happened and the lighter is broken up and gone. Two floes of exactly equal mass shatter each other, and both are lost. Floes drifting the same way never meet at all, since nothing ever catches anything up. The survey station wants to know how much ice will still be afloat once the strait settles.
problems.statement:
You are given the floes in order along the strait, from west to east. A positive number is a floe drifting east, a negative number one drifting west, and the size of the number is the floe’s mass in tonnes.

Two floes meet when one drifting east lies west of one drifting west, with nothing left between them. The heavier survives unchanged, the lighter is destroyed, and equal masses destroy both.

Return how many floes are still afloat once no further meetings are possible.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one floe, listed from the west end of the strait to the east. Its sign gives the direction it drifts, positive for east and negative for west, and its size gives its mass in tonnes. No floe has mass zero, and the strait may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: how many floes remain once the strait settles. Return 0 if none do.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: One entry per floe from west to east, signed for drift direction and sized by mass in tonnes.

constraints: 1 <= mass of every floe <= 1000000000, so every value lies between -1000000000 and 1000000000
No value is 0, because a floe always drifts one way or the other
All floes drift at the same speed, so two drifting the same way never meet

examples.explanation: The 12-tonne floe drifts east and meets the 4-tonne westbound floe, which is lighter and is destroyed. The 3- and 12-tonne floes both drift east, so they never meet, and two remain afloat.
The two floes are the same mass and close on each other, so they shatter each other and nothing is left afloat.
The 7-tonne westbound floe destroys the 3-tonne eastbound one, then meets the 15-tonne floe and is destroyed by it. Only the 15-tonne floe remains.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: the westbound floe loses to the 10-tonne floe.
One westbound floe destroys a lighter floe and then loses to a heavier one.
An empty strait. Catches a solution that assumes at least one floe or reads a first element unconditionally.
A single floe with nothing to meet, at the smallest mass allowed.
Both mass extremes, closing on each other and exactly equal, so both are destroyed. Catches a comparison that treats equal masses as a win for one side.

Nothing meets anything. The westbound floes are already west of the eastbound ones, so every pair is drifting apart. A solution that collides any adjacent pair of opposite sign without checking which side each is on reports fewer than four.
Two separate equal-mass meetings, one after the other. Catches a solution that stops simulating after the first time the strait empties.
One heavy westbound floe destroys three eastbound floes in a row and survives. Catches a solution that resolves only one meeting per incoming floe.

hints: Work along the strait from west to east and ask, for each floe in turn, whether it can still be destroyed by anything that comes later.
A westbound floe can only ever meet floes to its west, and only eastbound ones. Everything else is either drifting away from it or chasing it at the same speed.
The eastbound floes still in play are exactly the ones an incoming westbound floe has to fight, and it fights them nearest first. That ordering is what a stack gives you.

One incoming floe may destroy several in a row, so the fight is a loop rather than a single comparison, and it can end three ways: the incoming floe dies, it survives everything, or the strait behind it empties.
Equal masses destroy each other. That case removes two floes at once and is the one most easily written as a win for one side.

editorial.overview: Read the strait once from west to east, keeping the floes that are still afloat and could still be hit. A floe drifting west only ever meets eastbound floes lying to its west, nearest first, so the survivors behave exactly like a stack: the last one kept is the first one fought.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Simulate the strait in time steps, moving every floe and resolving collisions as they occur. Correct, but the number of steps depends on how far apart the floes start, which the input does not even give, and re-scanning the whole strait each step is quadratic at best.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a stack of the floes still afloat. For each floe in turn, if it drifts east, push it: nothing already kept can ever meet it, because everything to its west that is still afloat is either drifting west and moving away or drifting east at the same speed. If it drifts west, fight it against the top of the stack while that top is an eastbound floe. Pop the top when it is lighter and continue the fight; pop it and destroy the incoming floe when the masses are equal; destroy the incoming floe and stop when the top is heavier. If the fight empties the stack or reaches a westbound floe on top, the incoming floe survives and is pushed. Each floe is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the pass is O(n) time and O(n) space, and the answer is the size of the stack at the end.
editorial.correctnessProof: The stack holds exactly the floes that are still afloat and still able to be met, in west-to-east order, with every eastbound floe in it lying east of every floe that could destroy it. Two facts keep that true. An eastbound floe can never meet anything already in the stack, since a stacked eastbound floe drifts at the same speed and a stacked westbound floe is west of it and moving away, so pushing it preserves the invariant. A westbound floe can only meet the eastbound floes in the stack, and it reaches them in order from the top down, because the top is the nearest one to its west. Resolving that fight top-down therefore matches the order the meetings really happen in. Since each meeting removes at least one floe and no floe is ever added twice, the simulation terminates and its result is the true final state.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the number of floes. Each floe is pushed at most once and popped at most once across the whole pass.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the stack of surviving floes, which in the worst case holds every floe.

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Sixth hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. Stack simulation with pairwise elimination is a standard technique and is named openly in the editorial; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Two candidates were rejected under the distinctness rule because the group being replaced is largest-rectangle-in-histogram, the canonical monotonic-stack problem: trapping rain water reuses the same histogram input, the same previous-smaller and next-smaller machinery, and still answers with an area over a histogram, and sum of subarray minimums is built on that same prev/next-smaller pair. This record uses a stack to simulate rather than to aggregate over ranges, which is what makes it a different computation rather than a different story.

The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is k (one means the tail). values[1..] lists linked-list node values from head to tail.
problems.outputFormat: Return the value of the kth node from the end, or -1 when k is outside the chain.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: Node values fit in signed 32-bit integers.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated reverse-rank chain lookup process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 30.
Example 2 follows the stated reverse-rank chain lookup process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 8.

testCases.explanation: Applying the reverse-rank chain lookup rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the reverse-rank chain lookup rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Move a lead pointer k nodes before moving a second pointer.
When the lead pointer reaches the end, the second pointer has the requested reverse rank.

editorial.overview: Interpret the payload after k as a singly linked chain and keep a fixed gap between two positions.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Count all nodes, convert the reverse rank to a forward index, then traverse again.
editorial.optimalApproach: Advance a lead position k steps. If possible, advance lead and follower together until lead leaves the chain.
editorial.correctnessProof: The lead stays exactly k nodes ahead of the follower. When lead is one position beyond the tail, exactly k nodes including the follower remain from follower to tail, so follower is kth from the end.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(n<2||v[0]<1||v[0]>n-1)return -1;return v[n-(int)v[0]];}

def solve(v: list[int]) -> int:

problems.story: Decision Tree Levels is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise binary-tree depth result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Decision Tree Levels. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the binary-tree depth, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values is a level-order binary-tree array using -1 for a missing node. Children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-present-node path; an empty or missing root has depth 0.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: -1 marks absence and is not a node value
Every present non-root node has a present ancestor chain.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated binary-tree depth process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 3.
Example 2 follows the stated binary-tree depth process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 1.

testCases.explanation: Applying the binary-tree depth rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the binary-tree depth rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: A level-order index determines its tree level.
Scan present nodes and retain the largest level, or traverse breadth first.

editorial.overview: Visit each present level-order entry and determine its one-based depth from its heap index.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each present node, repeatedly move to its parent and count steps to the root.
editorial.optimalApproach: Scan indices once while tracking the next power-of-two level boundary, updating the maximum for present nodes.
editorial.correctnessProof: Heap indices [2^(d-1)-1, 2^d-2] are exactly depth d. Every present node is inspected and assigned its exact depth, so the maximum assigned depth equals the longest root-to-node path.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(!n||v[0]==-1)return 0;int d=1,next=1,b=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){if(i==next){d++;next=next*2+1;}if(v[i]!=-1&&d>b)b=d;}return b;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){if(v.empty()||v[0]==-1)return 0;int d=1,next=1,b=0;for(int i=0;i<(int)v.size();i++){if(i==next){d++;next=next*2+1;}if(v[i]!=-1)b=max(b,d);}return b;}

problems.title: One Counter Open
problems.story: A repair counter opens at nine with everyone already waiting outside. There is one member of staff and one counter, so customers are seen strictly one at a time, and nobody leaves before being seen. The branch is measured on the total time its queue spends in the building: every customer’s time counts, from the doors opening until they walk out, so the order the staff member calls people in is the only thing that changes the score.
problems.statement:
You are given how long each waiting customer takes to serve. You may call them in any order.

A customer’s time in the building runs from opening until their own service finishes: the service times of everyone called before them, plus their own. The counter is never idle and only one customer is served at a time.

Return the smallest achievable total of every customer’s time in the building.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is how many minutes one waiting customer takes to serve. They are listed in no particular order, and the queue may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest achievable total of every customer’s time in the building. Return 0 for an empty queue.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: How many minutes each waiting customer takes to serve, in no particular order.

constraints: The queue may be empty, in which case the answer is 0
The answer can exceed the range of a 32-bit signed integer: a full queue of long jobs totals over 100000000000000

examples.explanation: Calling them shortest first, as 1 then 3 then 4, the three leave at minute 1, minute 4 and minute 8, which totals 13. Calling them in the order given leaves them at 4, 5 and 8, totalling 17.
Taking the one-minute customer first, they leave at minute 1 and the other at minute 11, totalling 12. The other way round it is minute 10 and minute 11, totalling 21.
Identical service times, so the order changes nothing at all. The three customers leave at minutes 5, 10 and 15.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: shortest first gives 1, 4 and 8.
Two customers, and the order nearly halves the score.
An empty queue. Catches a solution that assumes at least one customer or reads a first element unconditionally.
The smallest non-empty queue, one customer at the shortest service time.

Seven hundred customers at the maximum service time. The total is 2453500000, just past the 32-bit signed limit, so an accumulator of the wrong width wraps to a plausible negative rather than failing loudly.
One input, two wrong orders caught. Serving in the order given totals 55, and so does serving longest first. Only shortest first gives 23.
Every service time identical, so every order scores the same 70.
Sorted to 2, 3, 5, 8 the customers leave at minutes 2, 5, 10 and 18.

hints: Write down the total for a small queue in two different orders. The difference will tell you which customer you want to call first.
A customer who is called early adds their service time to everyone still waiting behind them, not just to their own total.
That means a service time is effectively multiplied by how many customers are still in the building when it runs, including the customer themselves.
To keep the large multipliers on the small numbers, call the shortest service first. After that the answer is a single pass with a running clock.

editorial.overview: Each customer’s time in the building is the running total of every service called up to and including theirs, so the answer is the sum of those running totals. Serving the shortest job first minimises it, and the whole solution is a sort followed by one pass with a running clock. This problem needs no heap: the topic bundles heaps with greedy scheduling, and a sort is all the greedy here requires.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every order, compute the total for each, and keep the smallest. Correct, and hopeless past about ten customers, since the number of orders is the factorial of the queue length.
editorial.optimalApproach: Sort the service times ascending, then sweep once keeping a running clock. For each customer add their service to the clock, then add the clock to the answer. Sorting dominates, so this is O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the sorted copy. The accumulator must be 64-bit: with two hundred thousand customers at ten thousand minutes each the total passes ten to the fourteenth, which overflows a 32-bit integer silently.
editorial.correctnessProof: An exchange argument. Take any order and suppose two customers served one immediately after the other have service times a then b with a greater than b. Everyone before them is unaffected, and so is everyone after, because the pair finishes at the same moment either way. Only the pair changes: as a then b their two contributions are C plus a, and C plus a plus b, where C is the clock before the pair. Swapped, they are C plus b, and C plus b plus a. The second terms are equal and the first differs by a minus b, which is positive, so swapping to put the shorter job first strictly lowers the total. Any order that is not sorted ascending contains such an adjacent pair, so it can be improved; therefore the sorted order is optimal. Equal service times give a difference of zero, which is why ties can be broken arbitrarily.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n), where n is the number of customers. The sort dominates; the sweep that follows is linear.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sorted copy of the service times, or O(1) extra if the input may be sorted in place.

python3.referenceSolution:
def solve(values: list[int]) -> int:
    elapsed = 0
    total = 0
    for service in sorted(values):
        elapsed += service
        total += elapsed
    return total

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Fifth hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. Shortest-job-first scheduling and its exchange-argument proof are standard and named openly in the editorial, including the fact that no heap is required; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Designed as an easy problem because the free-slug check showed every unreferenced heap-greedy slot was easy, and relabelling to fit an occupied slot would be the cosmetic-difficulty fault D27 records. Calibration is plus one because the sort is easy to guess while the 64-bit accumulation is where solutions actually fail.

problems.title: Rope Splicing Bill
problems.story: A rigger has to splice a pile of loose ropes into one. Each splice joins two ropes into a single rope as long as both together, and the yard charges for the length of rope produced. The rigger wants the cheapest total bill.
problems.statement:
You are given the length of each loose rope.

Repeatedly splice any two ropes into one, paying their combined length each time, until at most one rope is left.

Return the smallest total you can pay. Nothing to splice costs 0.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is the length of one loose rope. There may be no ropes at all.
problems.outputFormat: Return the smallest total charge needed to leave at most one rope.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: The total cost fits in signed 64-bit range.

examples.explanation: Splice 2 and 5 into a 7 for a charge of 7, then the 7 and the 8 into a 15 for a charge of 15, giving 22. Starting with 5 and 8 would cost 13 then 15, which is 28.
A single splice joins the two ropes into one of length 18, and that 18 is the whole bill.

testCases.explanation: Applying the minimum repeated merge cost rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the minimum repeated merge cost rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: An expensive combined bundle may be charged again later.
Always combine the two smallest current bundles; a min-heap makes them available.

editorial.overview: Use the optimal merge pattern: repeatedly remove the two smallest sizes, add their sum to the cost, and insert the sum.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Explore every possible pair to merge at every stage and take the cheapest complete sequence.
editorial.optimalApproach: A min-heap implements the greedy choice of merging the two smallest current bundles.
editorial.correctnessProof: In an optimal merge tree, the two smallest weights can be made sibling leaves at greatest depth without increasing cost. Merging them reduces the problem to the same problem on one fewer bundle, so repeating the choice is optimal.

int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*(n?n:1));memcpy(a,v,sizeof(long long)*n);long long c=0;while(n>1){qsort(a,n,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);long long s=a[0]+a[1];c+=s;memmove(a,a+2,sizeof(long long)*(n-2));a[n-2]=s;n--;}free(a);return c;}

problems.title: Constellation Connection Groups
problems.story: Constellation Connection Groups is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise undirected connected components result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Constellation Connection Groups. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the undirected connected components, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is node count n. Remaining values are endpoint pairs for undirected edges over nodes 0..n-1.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of connected components, counting isolated nodes.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: The remaining input length is even
0 <= each edge endpoint < n; duplicate edges and self-loops may occur.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated undirected connected components process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.
Example 2 follows the stated undirected connected components process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 1.

testCases.explanation: Applying the undirected connected components rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the undirected connected components rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Begin with every node in its own group.
Union the endpoints of each edge and count how many roots remain.

editorial.overview: A disjoint-set union structure starts with n components and merges the roots of every edge.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: For each unvisited node, run a graph traversal and mark every reachable node.
editorial.optimalApproach: Union by representative with path compression; decrement the component count only when two roots differ.
editorial.correctnessProof: Initially each isolated node is one component. An edge between different representatives merges exactly two components and reduces the count by one; an edge inside one representative changes nothing. After all edges, representatives match graph connectivity.

int root(int*p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int z){if(!z)return 0;int n=(int)v[0],*p=malloc(sizeof(int)*n);for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;int c=n;for(int i=1;i+1<z;i+=2){int a=root(p,(int)v[i]),b=root(p,(int)v[i+1]);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;c--;}}free(p);return c;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){if(v.empty())return 0;int n=v[0];vector<int>p(n);iota(p.begin(),p.end(),0);function<int(int)>f=[&](int x){return p[x]==x?x:p[x]=f(p[x]);};int c=n;for(int i=1;i+1<(int)v.size();i+=2){int a=f(v[i]),b=f(v[i+1]);if(a!=b)p[a]=b,c--;}return c;}

java.referenceSolution: static int root(int[]p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}static long solve(long[]v){if(v.length==0)return 0;int n=(int)v[0],c=n;int[]p=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;for(int i=1;i+1<v.length;i+=2){int a=root(p,(int)v[i]),b=root(p,(int)v[i+1]);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;c--;}}return c;}

python3.referenceSolution:
def solve(v: list[int]) -> int:
    if not v:return 0
    n=v[0];p=list(range(n))
    def f(x):
        while p[x]!=x:p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x]
        return x
    c=n
    for i in range(1,len(v)-1,2):
        a,b=f(v[i]),f(v[i+1])
        if a!=b:p[a]=b;c-=1
    return c

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;const n=v[0],p=Array.from({length:n},(_,i)=>i);function f(x){while(p[x]!==x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}let c=n;for(let i=1;i+1<v.length;i+=2){const a=f(v[i]),b=f(v[i+1]);if(a!==b){p[a]=b;c--;}}return c;}

problems.statement: Implement the required function for Donation Target Subsets. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the target-sum subset count, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is a nonnegative target. Remaining nonnegative integers may each be selected at most once.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of index-distinct subsets whose sum is exactly target.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: 0 <= candidate value <= target; the answer fits signed 64-bit range.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated target-sum subset count process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.
Example 2 follows the stated target-sum subset count process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 1.

testCases.explanation: Applying the target-sum subset count rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the target-sum subset count rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Track how many selections produce each sum up to the target.
Update sums from high to low so one candidate is not reused in the same step.

editorial.overview: One-dimensional subset-sum dynamic programming counts index-distinct selections for every reachable sum.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Enumerate all 2^n subsets, compute each sum, and count those equal to target.
editorial.optimalApproach: Set ways[0] = 1. For each candidate, add ways[sum-value] into ways[sum] while iterating sums downward.
editorial.correctnessProof: Before a candidate, ways[s] counts subsets of earlier candidates totaling s. Downward updates add exactly the subsets formed by appending the current candidate, while retaining subsets that omit it. Thus the invariant holds after every candidate.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(!n)return 0;int t=v[0];long long*d=calloc(t+1,sizeof(long long));d[0]=1;for(int i=1;i<n;i++)for(int s=t;s>=v[i];s--)d[s]+=d[s-v[i]];long long a=d[t];free(d);return a;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){if(v.empty())return 0;int t=v[0];vector<long long>d(t+1);d[0]=1;for(int i=1;i<(int)v.size();i++)for(int s=t;s>=v[i];s--)d[s]+=d[s-v[i]];return d[t];}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){if(v.length==0)return 0;int t=(int)v[0];long[]d=new long[t+1];d[0]=1;for(int i=1;i<v.length;i++)for(int s=t;s>=v[i];s--)d[s]+=d[s-(int)v[i]];return d[t];}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;const t=v[0],d=Array(t+1).fill(0);d[0]=1;for(const x of v.slice(1))for(let s=t;s>=x;s--)d[s]+=d[s-x];return d[t];}

problems.title: Rising Corridor
problems.story: A gallery hangs its collection along a single corridor in the order the pieces were acquired. That ordering is a curatorial rule and cannot be changed: the corridor is meant to be read as a history, so a piece acquired later never hangs before one acquired earlier. The incoming director wants the corridor to read as a rising line, each piece on display taller than the one before it. Pieces that spoil the line can go to storage, but the ones that stay keep their relative order, because that is the rule that cannot bend.
problems.statement:
You are given the height of each piece, in acquisition order.

You may send any pieces to storage. The pieces left on display keep their original relative order. The display is a rising line if each piece on it is strictly taller than the piece before it, so two pieces of equal height can never both stay: neither is taller than the other.

Return the largest number of pieces that can stay on display.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is the height of one piece in millimetres, given in the order the pieces were acquired. The collection may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest number of pieces that can form a rising line without reordering them. Return 0 for an empty collection.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The height in millimetres of every piece, in the order the pieces were acquired.

constraints: Heights may repeat, and equal heights can never follow one another on the display
A quadratic solution will not finish inside the time limit at the top of this range

examples.explanation: Keeping the pieces of height 95, 210, 240 and 300 gives a rising line of four. Nothing longer exists: the 260 at the end is shorter than the 300 before it, so those two cannot both stay.
Four pieces of identical height. The line must rise strictly, so equal heights cannot follow one another and only a single piece can stay on display.
Every piece is shorter than the one before it, so no two can stay together. The best possible display holds one piece.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: 95, 210, 240, 300 is a rising line of four.
Equal heights cannot follow one another, so only one piece stays.
An empty collection. Catches a solution that assumes at least one piece, or seeds its answer at one.
The smallest non-empty collection, holding the shortest height allowed.
Both height extremes present. The first and last pieces are equal, so the answer pairs the short middle piece with one tall one.

One input, two wrong answers caught. A solution comparing with <= instead of < reports 5 by keeping both pieces of height 150. A solution measuring the longest run of consecutive positions rather than a subsequence reports 3 by taking only 160, 170, 180.
Strictly descending, the worst case for the answer. Every piece but one goes to storage.
The best line is the later, lower group 10, 20, 30, 40 rather than the earlier 50, 60, 70. A solution that commits to the first rising run it finds reports 3.

hints: Nothing is ever reordered, so the only decision is which pieces to keep. Storage is where the discarded ones go, not a place you can rearrange.
Fix the piece that ends the display. The best line ending there is one more than the best line ending at some earlier, strictly shorter piece.
That recurrence compares every piece with every earlier piece, which is quadratic and will not finish at two hundred thousand pieces. Ask what you actually need to remember from the earlier work.
For each possible line length, remember only the smallest height that can end a line of that length. Adding a piece either extends the longest line or improves one of those endings.
The list of smallest endings is always sorted, which is what lets you find the entry a new height belongs at with a binary search rather than a scan.

editorial.overview: Order is fixed and only removal is allowed, so the display is a subsequence of the acquisition order, and the rising rule makes it a strictly increasing one. The task is therefore the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, and the whole difficulty is getting that length without comparing every pair of pieces.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Let best[i] be the longest rising line that ends with piece i. Then best[i] is one plus the largest best[j] over every earlier piece j that is strictly shorter, or one if there is no such piece. The answer is the largest best[i]. This is correct and costs O(n squared), which is about four times ten to the tenth comparisons at the top of the range and will not finish.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a list called tails, where tails[k] is the smallest height that can end a rising line of length k plus one. This list is always strictly increasing: a line of length k plus one contains a line of length k ending at a strictly smaller height, so tails[k] is strictly below tails[k plus one]. For each incoming height, binary search for the first entry that is greater than or equal to it. If there is none, the height extends the longest line and is appended. Otherwise it replaces that entry, because a line of that length can now end at a smaller height, which can only help later pieces. The answer is the final length of tails. Each piece costs one binary search, so the whole pass is O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Note that tails is not itself a valid display; only its length is meaningful.
editorial.correctnessProof: Two claims. First, tails stays sorted and each entry is achievable: appending happens only when the new height exceeds every entry, which extends a real line by one, and replacing sets tails[k] to a height that ends a line of length k plus one because everything before position k is unchanged and still strictly smaller. Second, tails[k] is minimal. Suppose some rising line of length k plus one ended at a height below tails[k]. Consider the moment its last piece was processed. The binary search would have found the first entry greater than or equal to that height at index k or lower and written it there, so tails[k] would already be at most that height. Since every entry is achievable and no achievable ending is smaller, the length of tails is exactly the length of the longest rising line. Strictness is carried entirely by searching for the first entry greater than or equal to the height rather than strictly greater, which is what stops equal heights extending a line.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n), where n is the number of pieces. One binary search over a list of at most n entries per piece.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the list of smallest endings.

provenance.author: Vikram Yadav
provenance.note: Third hand-authored replacement for the generated library described in D27, written against docs/authoring-problems.md. The longest-increasing-subsequence pattern and its patience-sorting refinement are standard and named openly in the editorial; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Coin change and maximum subarray sum were both considered and rejected under the distinctness rule: the first belongs to the hit-a-target-from-a-set family the library already covers twice, the second to the maximise-a-sum-over-a-selection family of the group this record replaces.

problems.title: Orchard Row Harvest
problems.story: A hedge-row of fruit trees is picked once a season. Picking a tree makes its immediate neighbours unpickable that year, because the ladder crushes the roots. Each tree’s yield is known before the picking starts.
problems.statement:
You are given the yield of each tree, left to right along the row.

Choose any set of trees with no two of them next to each other, and return the greatest total yield those trees give.

An empty row yields 0.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one tree’s yield, in the order the trees stand along the row. The row may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return the greatest total yield obtainable without picking two neighbouring trees.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: The result fits in signed 64-bit range.

examples.explanation: Picking the second and fourth trees gives 10 + 8 = 18. The only other way to take more than two trees is the first, third and fifth, which reaches just 3 + 4 + 2 = 9.
The two outer trees are not neighbours, so both can be picked for 6 + 6 = 12. Picking the middle tree alone would yield only 1.

testCases.explanation: Applying the maximum nonadjacent total rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the maximum nonadjacent total rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: At each position, compare skipping it with taking it after the best result two positions back.
Only the previous two dynamic-programming states are needed.

editorial.overview: Use the recurrence best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + values[i]) with two rolling variables.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Recursively choose or skip every position, rejecting branches that choose adjacent positions.
editorial.optimalApproach: Maintain the best total through the previous position and through the position before it, updating once per reward.
editorial.correctnessProof: Every valid optimal selection either omits the current position, giving the previous best, or includes it, forcing omission of the previous position and giving the two-back best plus current reward. Taking the maximum covers both exhaustive cases.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){long long a=0,b=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){long long z=b>a+v[i]?b:a+v[i];a=b;b=z;}return b;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){long long a=0,b=0;for(auto x:v){auto n=max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){long a=0,b=0;for(long x:v){long n=Math.max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){let a=0,b=0;for(const x of v){const n=Math.max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}
